demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
I remind myself it could have been worse
try hard not think about the trauma

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
issues.explanation: Water/flooding triggers are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of accidentally causing serious injury to another in a car accident, given the rest of the profile centers on crash-related and guilt/shame themes. This trigger introduces a different threat context without support from memory or appraisal items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Feelings: Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Feelings' is internally incoherent as worded: 'Allowing myself to feel any strong emotion' describes the opposite of avoidance. Within the maladaptive strategies node, it directly conflicts with an avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' fits poorly with the rest of the profile for a perpetration-type accident trauma in which the patient's appraisals otherwise center on guilt, humiliation, and shattered beliefs. There are no memory, trigger, or strategy items suggesting bodily injury, panic/somatic threat, or physical incapacity to support this appraisal.

vignette: Amir, a 42-year-old Indian American tax inspector, recalls the moment that turned his life from routine to haunting with a clarity that feels more cinematic than lived. He was driving home after a long day of filing returns, when a delivery truck, swerving to avoid a sudden pothole, spun and collided with his sedan. The crash left a fellow driver severely injured, and Amir was immediately flooded with a chorus of sound-the crunch of metal, the scream of a passenger, and the hiss of air-bag inflation. He was later diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, scoring 72 on the PCL-5, and his symptoms have grown entrenched over the past two years. The images of cars smashing together have become a constant, invisible trigger. Whenever Amir's supervisor shows a slide of traffic statistics on the office screen, he feels the memory flash back so vividly that he involuntarily withdraws his hand from the keyboard, forcing a pause in his work. This withdrawal is not merely a reflex; the trigger directly leads him into his self-punishing thoughts. He tells himself that he deserves to suffer because of what happened, that he should have protected the other driver, and that life is unforgivable. Those thoughts, in turn, deepen his sense of humiliation and reinforce his conviction that he has failed. He has learned to suppress any conversation about the crash, hoping that not thinking about it will make the memory fade, but the very act of trying to push the images away only amplifies their presence. The cycle of trigger, punishment thinking, and heightened shame is so relentless that Amir often avoids even looking at news reports of car accidents while on his commute, and he has begun to skip over traffic updates that appear in his tax-audit briefing videos. Each avoidance tactic feeds back into the trigger loop, making him more sensitive to the same images he tried to escape. Amir's recollection of the day is fragmentary. Some moments-such as the sudden jolt of the car and the scream-are etched in his mind with crystalline clarity, while other parts blur into nothingness. He often hears, in his head, the same radio chatter he heard that day, as if the auditory cues are replaying the trauma in real time. He feels as though he is only remembering bits of what happened and that the rest is missing. This sense of an incomplete picture is not a passive feeling; his humiliation and belief that the world no longer makes sense make him question the reliability of the memory itself. In the quiet moments at home, he tries to piece together the timeline, but the gaps only widen his fear that he may have misjudged what he should have done. The way his self-punishing thoughts shape how he recalls the event-blurring some parts and sharpening others-feeds directly into his distorted appraisal of the world and his role in it. Over the months, these patterns have carved a niche in Amir's daily routine. When he hears a car honk outside the office, his mind rushes to the crash, and he automatically thinks, "I should have been more careful." That thought, coupled with the feeling that he has disgraced himself, pulls him further into shame, which, in turn, sharpens the images whenever he sees a car crash or a funeral notice. He now avoids family gatherings that include funeral urns, fearing that the sight of a gravesite will bring back the memory and the accompanying humiliation. His marriage has strained; he has stopped sharing his thoughts with his wife, fearing she will see him as weak. He has even begun to question whether his job, which requires him to review and analyze financial reports-often containing numbers that look like car registration plates-has become a constant source of trigger. Amir finally decided to seek help after a particularly harrowing night. While scrolling through a memorial page on social media, a photograph of a burial plot appeared in his feed. The image sent a shockwave of guilt and the feeling that he had abandoned his role as a protector. He realized that the self-disciplining thoughts were no longer just internal monologues but were actively shaping his reality, making his days feel like a living nightmare. He is terrified that the cycle will continue to erode his sense of self and that his career might suffer if he cannot manage the triggers. Yet, he also holds a quiet hope that by breaking the loop, he can reclaim his life, regain trust in himself, and protect his loved ones from the weight of his own guilt.
